# How To cite

# Input Excel file

The working Excel file serves as both the input and output container for the entire procedure. It must contain the following sheets:

**`Spec`** — Defines the label levels and their probabilities. Required columns: `n_items` (total number of items, entered only in the first row), `Label` (one row per label level), and `Proportion` (relative frequency of each label, need not sum exactly to 1 as it is renormalised automatically). This sheet has two distinct roles. Module 1 uses it to generate a synthetic corpus. Module 2 reads it again to build `probs_k`, the probability vector that Module 3 passes to the random generator — which is what selects the simulation scenario. It is therefore read on every run, including when Module 1 is bypassed.

**`Corpus`** — Contains the labelled dataset. Required columns: `ID` (unique item identifier) and `Label` (category assigned to each item). Optional columns: `Title` and `Abstract`. This sheet is written by Module 1 if generating a synthetic corpus, or populated manually by the user if working with a real dataset. If this sheet already contains data when Module 1 runs, synthetic generation is skipped entirely.

**`Simulations`** — Receives the simulated classification vectors produced by Module 3, one column per iteration. Leave blank before the first run. Module 3 overwrites this sheet every time it is executed; to reuse an existing set of simulations, do not execute Module 3 and go straight to Module 4, which reads whatever the sheet contains.

**`Reporting`** — Receives the metric summary table produced by Module 4. Overwritten on each run.

The file can be used in two ways: starting from a `Spec`-only file with an empty `Corpus` sheet (synthetic mode, run all modules in order), or starting from a file with a pre-populated `Corpus` sheet (real dataset mode, skip Module 1).

# Scenarios

The procedure defines two scenarios, and neither is hard-coded: the scenario is determined entirely by the `Proportion` column of the `Spec` sheet, which becomes the probability vector `probs_k` used by the random generator in Module 3. Use one Excel file per scenario and run the pipeline once for each.

**Scenario A — uniform.** Set `Proportion` to 1/k for every label level (0.5 and 0.5 in the binary case). Each record receives a label with probability 1/k regardless of the label distribution of the gold standard. This is the purest chance reference and the most conservative scenario: it answers what performance to expect from a classifier assigning labels at random with no knowledge of the corpus distribution.

**Scenario B — informed by the gold standard.** Set `Proportion` to the observed frequency of each label in the reference coder's classification (for example 0.118 and 0.882 for a corpus with 11.8% prevalence). Each record receives a label with probability proportional to that frequency. This answers what performance to expect from a classifier that reproduces the label distribution of the gold standard while having no genuine discriminative capacity, and is the scenario most directly comparable with real classifiers.

The two files should be identical except for that column, with the same `Corpus` sheet in both. Module 2 prints the loaded distribution and the corpus prevalence separately, so the scenario in force can be verified before simulating: under Scenario B the two coincide, under Scenario A they do not.

**One caveat when generating a synthetic corpus.** `Proportion` then does double duty — it fixes the true labels written by Module 1 *and* the simulated labels drawn by Module 3. Running Module 1 with a uniform Spec produces a balanced gold standard, which is not what Scenario A describes. To test Scenario A on an imbalanced corpus, generate the corpus first with the imbalanced Spec, then edit `Proportion` to uniform before running Module 3. With a real corpus the question does not arise, since Module 1 is bypassed and `Spec` only feeds the simulation.

# Module 0 — Setup & file selection

This module handles all session-level configuration. It installs and loads any missing packages, defines all global parameters (file names, label mappings, iteration count, random seed, and sheet names), and resolves the path to the working Excel file. Path resolution follows a three-step priority: if `EXCEL_PATH` is explicitly set and the file exists, it is used directly; if only `EXCEL_FILE` is provided, the path is built from the `.qmd` directory; if neither is set or the file is not found, a native RStudio file picker dialog opens. All downstream modules consume `EXCEL_PATH` without modification.

```{r module-00-setup}

# ******************************************
# Packages
# ******************************************
.ensure_packages <- function(pkgs) {
  missing <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
  if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  invisible(lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))
}

.ensure_packages(c("openxlsx", "dplyr", "purrr", "tibble", "rstudioapi"))
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Parameters
# ******************************************
EXCEL_PATH <- NULL          # "C:/full/path/to/file.xlsx"  |  NULL → resolve below
EXCEL_FILE <- "ART760_templateN-200.xlsx"        # "ART760_template.xlsx"  "ART760_templateN-200.xlsx"  |  NULL → without "" file picker
POS_LABELS <- "included"   # label(s) mapped to POSITIVE — use c("a","b") for multiple
NEG_LABELS <- "excluded"   # label(s) mapped to NEGATIVE — use c("a","b") for multiple
N_ITER     <- 10000L    # L forces R to save number as integer (more semantic congruence for counters and less memory)
SEED       <- 34L       # Comment if no Seed Needed L forces R to save number as integer (more semantic congruence for counters and less memory)

SH_SPEC <- "Spec"
SH_CORP <- "Corpus"
SH_SIMS <- "Simulations"
SH_REP  <- "Reporting"
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Resolve Excel path
# ******************************************
script_dir <- tryCatch(
  dirname(rstudioapi::getSourceEditorContext()$path),
  error = function(e) getwd()
)

.resolve_excel <- function(excel_path, filename, dir) {

  # 1. Full path provided and valid → use directly
  if (!is.null(excel_path) && nzchar(excel_path)) {
    if (!file.exists(excel_path)) stop("EXCEL_PATH not found: ", excel_path)
    message("✔ Using EXCEL_PATH: ", excel_path)
    return(excel_path)
  }

  # 2. Filename provided → build path from script_dir
  if (!is.null(filename) && nzchar(filename)) {
    full_path <- file.path(dir, filename)
    if (file.exists(full_path)) {
      message("✔ File found: ", basename(full_path))
      return(full_path)
    }
    message("⚠ '", filename, "' not found in ", dir, ". Opening file picker…")
  }

  # 3. Neither provided or file not found → native file picker
  chosen <- rstudioapi::selectFile(
    caption = "Select the scenario Excel file",
    path    = dir,
    filter  = "Excel files (*.xlsx)"
  )
  if (is.null(chosen) || !nzchar(chosen)) stop("No file selected.")
  if (!file.exists(chosen))               stop("File not found: ", chosen)

  message("✔ Selected: ", basename(chosen))
  chosen
}

EXCEL_PATH <- .resolve_excel(EXCEL_PATH, EXCEL_FILE, script_dir)
message("   Working directory: ", script_dir)
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Spec freezing
# ******************************************
# openxlsx preserves formulas but discards their cached values when a workbook
# is re-saved, so a formula in Spec becomes unreadable in any file this notebook
# writes. Called before the first save of each path, this replaces the sheet
# with the literal numbers already held in spec_df; every later save then
# preserves them, because they are no longer formulas.
.freeze_spec <- function(wb) {
  if (exists("spec_df") && SH_SPEC %in% names(wb))
    openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_SPEC, spec_df, startRow = 1, colNames = TRUE)
  invisible(wb)
}
# ******************************************

```

# Module 1 — Synthetic corpus generation

This module generates a synthetic labelled corpus from the parameters defined in the `Spec` sheet and writes it to the `Corpus` sheet of a new Excel file. It is intended for testing and validation purposes before applying the procedure to a real dataset. The module first checks whether the `Corpus` sheet already contains data — if so, it skips execution entirely and preserves the current `EXCEL_PATH`. If the corpus is empty, it reads `n_items`, label names, and proportions from `Spec`, generates a randomised label vector respecting the specified distribution, and writes the resulting corpus to a new file named `[original]_synthetic.xlsx`, updating `EXCEL_PATH` accordingly so all subsequent modules point to the correct file.

```{r module-01-synth-corpus}
# Generates a synthetic corpus from the Spec sheet and writes it to the Corpus
# sheet. Automatically skipped if Corpus already contains data.

# ******************************************
# Check — skip if Corpus already has data
# ******************************************
.corpus_existing <- tryCatch(
  openxlsx::read.xlsx(EXCEL_PATH, sheet = SH_CORP),
  error = function(e) NULL
)

.skip_m1 <- !is.null(.corpus_existing) && nrow(.corpus_existing) > 0

if (.skip_m1) {
  message("⚠ Module 1 skipped: Corpus sheet already contains ",
          nrow(.corpus_existing), " rows. Proceed to Module 2.")
  message("  Label distribution in existing corpus:")
  print(as.data.frame(dplyr::count(.corpus_existing, Label)))
}

rm(.corpus_existing)
# ******************************************

if (!.skip_m1) {

  # ******************************************
  # Read Spec
  # ******************************************
  spec_df <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(EXCEL_PATH, sheet = SH_SPEC)
  
  required_spec <- c("n_items", "Label", "Proportion")
  missing_spec  <- setdiff(required_spec, names(spec_df))
  if (length(missing_spec))
    stop("Spec sheet missing columns: ", paste(missing_spec, collapse = ", "))
  
  spec_df  <- spec_df |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(Label), !is.na(Proportion))
  
  n_items  <- as.integer(spec_df$n_items[1])
  levels_k <- spec_df$Label
  probs_k  <- spec_df$Proportion / sum(spec_df$Proportion)
  
  if (abs(sum(spec_df$Proportion) - 1) > 0.01)
    warning("Spec proportions did not sum to 1 — renormalised automatically.")
  
  message("Spec loaded: ", n_items, " items | ",
          length(levels_k), " labels: ",
          paste(levels_k, round(probs_k, 3), sep = "=", collapse = " | "))
  # ******************************************

  # ******************************************
  # Generate synthetic corpus
  # ******************************************
  set.seed(SEED)

  counts    <- round(probs_k * n_items)
  counts[1] <- n_items - sum(counts[-1])

  label_vec    <- sample(rep(levels_k, times = counts))
  corpus_synth <- tibble::tibble(
    ID       = seq_len(n_items),
    Title    = paste("Synthetic reference", seq_len(n_items)),
    Abstract = paste("Abstract placeholder for item", seq_len(n_items)),
    Label    = label_vec
  )

  message("Synthetic corpus generated:")
  print(dplyr::count(corpus_synth, Label), n = Inf)
  # ******************************************

  # ******************************************
  # Write to Excel
  # ******************************************
  wb <- openxlsx::loadWorkbook(EXCEL_PATH)

  if (SH_CORP %in% names(wb)) openxlsx::removeWorksheet(wb, SH_CORP)
  openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, SH_CORP)

  hs <- openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold",
                               fgFill = "#E2EFDA", border = "Bottom")
  openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_CORP, corpus_synth, headerStyle = hs)
  openxlsx::setColWidths(wb, SH_CORP, cols = seq_len(ncol(corpus_synth)),
                          widths = "auto")

  synth_path <- sub("\\.xlsx$", "_synthetic.xlsx", EXCEL_PATH, ignore.case = TRUE)
  .freeze_spec(wb)
  openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, synth_path, overwrite = TRUE)
  EXCEL_PATH <- synth_path
  message("✔ Synthetic corpus written to '", basename(EXCEL_PATH), "'")
  # ******************************************

}
```

# Module 2 — Corpus reading & validation

This module reads the `Corpus` and `Spec` sheets from the working Excel file and prepares all objects required by the simulation and reporting modules. It validates that the mandatory columns (`ID` and `Label`) are present in the corpus, warns about missing optional columns (`Title`, `Abstract`), and checks that all label values can be mapped to the binary positive/negative scheme defined by `POS_LABELS` and `NEG_LABELS` in Module 0. Any unmapped label is flagged with a warning and set to `NA` in `label_bin`. The Spec sheet is also read and validated here, with proportions renormalised if they do not sum exactly to 1. The module closes with a corpus summary showing total items, positive and negative counts with percentages, and the imbalance ratio.

This module is kept separate from Module 1 for two reasons. First, when working with a real dataset the user populates the `Corpus` sheet manually and skips Module 1 entirely — Module 2 is then the natural entry point of the pipeline. Second, separating reading and validation from simulation makes it easy to re-run the validation step in isolation if the corpus or label mappings change without triggering the simulation again.

```{r module-02-read-validate}
# Reads and validates the Corpus and Spec sheets. Binarises labels into
# positive / negative. Outputs corpus_df, spec_df, n_items, levels_k, probs_k.

# ******************************************
# Read Corpus
# ******************************************
corpus_raw <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(EXCEL_PATH, sheet = SH_CORP)

required_cols <- c("ID", "Label")
optional_cols <- c("Title", "Abstract")

missing_req <- setdiff(required_cols, names(corpus_raw))
if (length(missing_req))
  stop("Corpus sheet missing required columns: ", paste(missing_req, collapse = ", "))

missing_opt <- setdiff(optional_cols, names(corpus_raw))
if (length(missing_opt))
  warning("Corpus sheet missing optional columns: ", paste(missing_opt, collapse = ", "))

message("Corpus loaded: ", nrow(corpus_raw), " rows | ",
        ncol(corpus_raw), " columns")
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Binarise labels
# ******************************************
unknown_labels <- setdiff(unique(corpus_raw$Label), c(POS_LABELS, NEG_LABELS))
if (length(unknown_labels))
  warning("Unknown label(s) — will be set to NA in label_bin: ",
          paste(unknown_labels, collapse = ", "))

corpus_df <- corpus_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label_bin = dplyr::case_when(
      Label %in% POS_LABELS ~ "positive",
      Label %in% NEG_LABELS ~ "negative",
      TRUE                  ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

n_pos <- sum(corpus_df$label_bin == "positive", na.rm = TRUE)
n_neg <- sum(corpus_df$label_bin == "negative", na.rm = TRUE)
n_na  <- sum(is.na(corpus_df$label_bin))

message("Label binarisation: ", n_pos, " positive | ",
        n_neg, " negative | ", n_na, " NA")
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Read Spec
# ******************************************
spec_df <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(EXCEL_PATH, sheet = SH_SPEC)

required_spec <- c("n_items", "Label", "Proportion")
missing_spec  <- setdiff(required_spec, names(spec_df))
if (length(missing_spec))
  stop("Spec sheet missing columns: ", paste(missing_spec, collapse = ", "))

# A row with a Label but no Proportion means the value could not be read. The
# usual cause is a formula: re-saving a workbook keeps the formula but discards
# its cached result, so the cell comes back empty. Report which rows are affected
# instead of silently dropping them below.
.broken <- which(!is.na(spec_df$Label) & is.na(spec_df$Proportion))
if (length(.broken))
  stop("Spec sheet: Proportion is empty for ",
       paste0("'", spec_df$Label[.broken], "' (row ", .broken + 1L, ")",
              collapse = ", "),
       ". If those cells contain formulas, replace them with literal numbers — ",
       "a workbook re-saved by this notebook keeps the formula but loses its ",
       "cached value. Opening the file in Excel and saving it once also works.")
rm(.broken)

# Remove empty rows (n_items is only filled in the first row by design)
spec_df <- spec_df |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Label), !is.na(Proportion))

if (!nrow(spec_df))
  stop("Spec sheet has no usable rows: Label and Proportion are both empty.")

n_items  <- as.integer(spec_df$n_items[1])
levels_k <- spec_df$Label
probs_k  <- spec_df$Proportion / sum(spec_df$Proportion)

if (abs(sum(spec_df$Proportion) - 1) > 0.01)
  warning("Spec proportions did not sum to 1 — renormalised automatically.")

message("Spec loaded: ", length(levels_k), " label levels | ",
        paste(levels_k, round(probs_k, 3), sep = "=", collapse = " | "))
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Corpus summary
# ******************************************
message("─── Corpus summary ───────────────────────────────")
message("  Total items   : ", nrow(corpus_df))
message("  Positive (n)  : ", n_pos, " (", round(n_pos / nrow(corpus_df) * 100, 1), "%)")
message("  Negative (n)  : ", n_neg, " (", round(n_neg / nrow(corpus_df) * 100, 1), "%)")
message("  NA label_bin  : ", n_na)
message("  Imbalance ratio (neg/pos): ", round(n_neg / n_pos, 2))
message("──────────────────────────────────────────────────")
# ******************************************
```

# Module 3 — Monte Carlo simulation

This module generates N_ITER simulated classification vectors for the corpus, using the label distribution defined in the Spec sheet (levels_k and probs_k). Each iteration produces one random classification of all items, stored as a column (iter_0001, iter_0002, …) with ID as the first column. Results are written to the Simulations sheet, overwriting any existing data. If you want to preserve a previous simulation run and proceed directly to Module 4, simply do not execute this chunk.

Sampling model (documentation)
The sampling model is defined by the call sample(lvls, size = n_rows * n_iter, replace = TRUE, prob = prob). With replace = TRUE and a fixed probability vector, every cell of the matrix is drawn independently, with no constraint on how many positive labels occur in a given iteration. The number of positives per iteration is therefore a random variable, not a fixed quantity.

This is deliberate. Drawing a fixed number of positive labels without replacement and permuting them across records would define a hypergeometric model instead, whose dispersion carries a finite population correction. The analytic expressions used to interpret the results assume the Bernoulli model implemented here. The draw is performed in a single call for the whole matrix, so draws are independent both across records (within an iteration) and across iterations.

When lvls has more than two levels, each draw is categorical rather than Bernoulli. After the binarisation applied in Module 2, the outcome is Bernoulli with probability equal to the sum of the probabilities of the categories mapped to the positive group. In the example corpus lvls has two levels, so the draw is Bernoulli directly.

This has a consequence for the metrics. Recall is computed over the m gold standard positives, which are fixed by the corpus. Under this model the number of true positives is Binomial(m, q), where q is the probability of the positive label in the active scenario, so the standard deviation of recall under chance is sqrt(q * (1 - q) / m). Dispersion is governed by m rather than by the total number of records.

```{r module-03-simulate}
# Generates N_ITER simulated classification vectors and writes them to the
# Simulations sheet (overwrites any existing data).
# To skip simulation and reuse a previous run: do NOT execute this chunk.

# ******************************************
# Simulation generator
# ******************************************
# Single source of truth for how simulated classifications are generated.
# Reused by module-05-stability. Do not duplicate this logic elsewhere.
.simulate_matrix <- function(n_iter, seed,
                             n_rows = nrow(corpus_df),
                             lvls   = levels_k,
                             prob   = probs_k) {
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- matrix(
    sample(lvls, size = n_rows * n_iter, replace = TRUE, prob = prob),
    nrow = n_rows, ncol = n_iter
  )
  colnames(m) <- sprintf("iter_%04d", seq_len(n_iter))
  m
}
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Run simulation
# ******************************************
message("Running ", N_ITER, " iterations × ", nrow(corpus_df), " items…")

.sim_matrix <- .simulate_matrix(n_iter = N_ITER, seed = SEED)

sims_df <- tibble::tibble(ID = corpus_df$ID,
                          as.data.frame(.sim_matrix))
rm(.sim_matrix)

message("✔ Simulation complete: ", nrow(sims_df), " items × ",
        N_ITER, " iterations")

# ******************************************
# Write to Excel
# ******************************************
message("Writing to Excel…")

wb <- openxlsx::loadWorkbook(EXCEL_PATH)

if (SH_SIMS %in% names(wb)) openxlsx::removeWorksheet(wb, SH_SIMS)
openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, SH_SIMS)

hs <- openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold",
                             fgFill = "#FFF2CC", border = "Bottom")
openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_SIMS, sims_df, headerStyle = hs)

.freeze_spec(wb)
openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, EXCEL_PATH, overwrite = TRUE)
message("✔ Simulations written to sheet '", SH_SIMS, "' in ",
        basename(EXCEL_PATH))
# ******************************************
```

# \[OPTIONAL\] Validation module — Known-case simulation

This module is not part of the main pipeline and does not affect any results. It is designed to verify that the metric calculations in Module 4 are correct by constructing four classification vectors with known outcomes: all_positive (every item classified as positive), all_negative (every item classified as negative), perfect (identical to the gold standard), and random_fair (random 50/50 assignment regardless of corpus prevalence). These four vectors overwrite the Simulations sheet and are loaded as sims_df so that Module 4 can be run immediately after without any other change. Run this module, then Module 4, then the Validation check module below.

```{r validation-known-cases}
# VALIDATION MODULE — not part of the main pipeline.
# Generates four known-outcome vectors and overwrites the Simulations sheet
# so Module 4 can be run to verify metric calculations.
#
# Expected results:
#   all_positive : Recall=1, Specificity=0, Precision=prevalence, MCC=0
#   all_negative : Recall=0, Specificity=1, Precision=NA,         MCC=0
#   perfect      : all metrics=1, MCC=1
#   random_fair  : BalancedAccuracy≈0.5, MCC≈0

# ******************************************
# Build validation vectors
# ******************************************
set.seed(SEED)
n <- nrow(corpus_df)

val_df <- tibble::tibble(
  ID           = corpus_df$ID,
  all_positive = POS_LABELS[1],
  all_negative = NEG_LABELS[1],
  perfect      = corpus_df$Label,
  random_fair  = sample(c(POS_LABELS[1], NEG_LABELS[1]),
                        size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.5))
)

message("Validation dataset built: ", n, " items × 4 cases")
message("  all_positive : all items classified as '", POS_LABELS[1], "'")
message("  all_negative : all items classified as '", NEG_LABELS[1], "'")
message("  perfect      : identical to gold standard")
message("  random_fair  : random 50/50 regardless of prevalence")
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Overwrite Simulations sheet
# ******************************************
wb <- openxlsx::loadWorkbook(EXCEL_PATH)

if (SH_SIMS %in% names(wb)) openxlsx::removeWorksheet(wb, SH_SIMS)
openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, SH_SIMS)

hs <- openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold",
                              fgFill = "#FFE0CC", border = "Bottom")
openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_SIMS, val_df, headerStyle = hs)
openxlsx::setColWidths(wb, SH_SIMS, cols = seq_len(ncol(val_df)),
                        widths = "auto")

openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, EXCEL_PATH, overwrite = TRUE)

# Expose as sims_df so Module 4 can consume it directly
sims_df <- val_df

message("✔ Validation cases written to '", SH_SIMS, "' and loaded as sims_df")
message("  → Now run Module 4 to verify metrics")
# ******************************************
```

# Module 4 — Metric computation & reporting

This module computes eight classification metrics — Recall, Specificity, Precision, NPV, F1, F2, Balanced Accuracy, and MCC — for each simulated iteration in `sims_df`. For each iteration, the simulated label vector is binarised into positive/negative using the same mapping defined in Module 0, the confusion matrix is computed against the gold standard `label_bin` from `corpus_df`, and the eight metrics are derived. Degenerate cases where the denominator is zero are handled explicitly and recorded as `NA`. Once all iterations are processed, the empirical distribution of each metric is summarised with mean, median, standard deviation, and a 95% confidence interval computed by the percentile method (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles). The summary table is written to the `Reporting` sheet and stored as `report_df` in the global environment.

## Interpreting the results

The output of this module is not a measure of classifier performance — it is the empirical baseline that a random classifier would achieve given the label distribution of the corpus. Two results serve as internal sanity checks: Balanced Accuracy should converge to 0.50 and MCC should converge to 0 as the number of iterations increases, since a random classifier has no discriminative capacity. Deviations from these values in small iteration runs (e.g. 10 iterations) are expected due to sampling variance and will stabilise at 10,000 iterations. The 95% CI quantifies the range within which a random classifier would fall 95% of the time — any real classifier scoring above the upper bound of Recall, F1, or Balanced Accuracy can be considered to beat chance for that metric. The NA percentage reported for F1 and F2 reflects iterations where the simulated classifier assigned no positive labels at all, a degenerate but statistically possible outcome under low-prevalence distributions that disappears with sufficient iterations.

```{r module-04-report}
# Computes 8 classification metrics for each simulation iteration,
# then summarises the empirical distribution with mean, median, SD and
# 95% CI by percentile method. Writes results to the Reporting sheet.

# ******************************************
# Helper functions
# ******************************************
.binarise <- function(x, pos, neg) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    x %in% pos ~ "positive",
    x %in% neg ~ "negative",
    TRUE        ~ NA_character_
  )
}

.confusion <- function(pred, truth) {
  list(
    tp = sum(pred == "positive" & truth == "positive", na.rm = TRUE),
    tn = sum(pred == "negative" & truth == "negative", na.rm = TRUE),
    fp = sum(pred == "positive" & truth == "negative", na.rm = TRUE),
    fn = sum(pred == "negative" & truth == "positive", na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

.metrics <- function(cm) {
  with(cm, {
    recall  <- if ((tp + fn) > 0) tp / (tp + fn)         else NA_real_
    spec    <- if ((tn + fp) > 0) tn / (tn + fp)         else NA_real_
    prec    <- if ((tp + fp) > 0) tp / (tp + fp)         else NA_real_
    npv     <- if ((tn + fn) > 0) tn / (tn + fn)         else NA_real_
    f1      <- if (!is.na(prec) && !is.na(recall) &&
                   (prec + recall) > 0)
                 2 * prec * recall / (prec + recall)      else NA_real_
    f2      <- if (!is.na(prec) && !is.na(recall) &&
                   (4 * prec + recall) > 0)
                 5 * prec * recall / (4 * prec + recall)  else NA_real_
    bal_acc <- if (!is.na(recall) && !is.na(spec))
                 (recall + spec) / 2                      else NA_real_
    # as.numeric() applied to each factor before multiplication prevents integer
    # overflow (R integers are capped at 2^31). Without it, large corpora cause
    # the product to exceed the integer limit and return NA.
    mcc_den <- sqrt(as.numeric(tp+fp) * as.numeric(tp+fn)*as.numeric(tn+fp) * as.numeric(tn+fn))
    mcc     <- if (mcc_den > 0) (tp*tn - fp*fn) / mcc_den else NA_real_

    c(Recall = recall, Specificity = spec, Precision = prec, NPV = npv,
      F1 = f1, F2 = f2, BalancedAccuracy = bal_acc, MCC = mcc)
  })
}

.metrics_table <- function(pred_cols, truth_vec) {
  # pred_cols: data frame or list where each element is one prediction vector.
  # Single source of truth for assembling the per-iteration metrics table.
  # Reused by module-05-stability.
  purrr::map(pred_cols, function(x) {
    .metrics(.confusion(.binarise(x, POS_LABELS, NEG_LABELS), truth_vec))
  }) |>
    (\(z) as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, z)))()
}

# Single source of truth for the percentile-method confidence interval.
.ci_lo <- function(vals) unname(quantile(vals, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE))
.ci_hi <- function(vals) unname(quantile(vals, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))

# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Compute metrics per iteration
# ******************************************
truth     <- corpus_df$label_bin
iter_cols <- setdiff(names(sims_df), "ID")

message("Computing metrics for ", length(iter_cols), " iterations…")

metrics_mat <- .metrics_table(sims_df[iter_cols], truth)

message("✔ Metrics computed: ", nrow(metrics_mat), " iterations × ",
        ncol(metrics_mat), " metrics")
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Summarise empirical distributions
# ******************************************
metric_names <- c("Recall", "Specificity", "Precision", "NPV",
                   "F1", "F2", "BalancedAccuracy", "MCC")

report_df <- purrr::map_dfr(metric_names, function(m) {
  vals <- metrics_mat[, m]
  tibble::tibble(
    Metric   = m,
    Mean     = mean(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median   = median(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD       = sd(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    CI95_Lo  = .ci_lo(vals),
    CI95_Hi  = .ci_hi(vals),
    NA_pct   = round(mean(is.na(vals)) * 100, 1)
  )
})

message("─── Empirical baseline summary ───────────────────")
print(as.data.frame(report_df))
message("──────────────────────────────────────────────────")
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Write to Excel
# ******************************************
wb <- openxlsx::loadWorkbook(EXCEL_PATH)

if (SH_REP %in% names(wb)) openxlsx::removeWorksheet(wb, SH_REP)
openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, SH_REP)

hs <- openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold",
                              fgFill = "#DCE6F1", border = "Bottom")
num_style <- openxlsx::createStyle(numFmt = "0.0000")

openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_REP, report_df, headerStyle = hs)
openxlsx::addStyle(wb, SH_REP, num_style,
                    rows = 2:(nrow(report_df) + 1),
                    cols = 2:(ncol(report_df) - 1),
                    gridExpand = TRUE)
openxlsx::setColWidths(wb, SH_REP, cols = seq_len(ncol(report_df)),
                        widths = "auto")

openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, EXCEL_PATH, overwrite = TRUE)
message("✔ Report written to sheet '", SH_REP, "' in ", basename(EXCEL_PATH))
# ******************************************
```

# Module 5 — Iteration-count sufficiency check

The default of 10,000 iterations is a convention, not a derivation. This module verifies empirically that it is sufficient for the corpus at hand. The user declares a target precision on the metric scale before running the check — the default of 0.01 follows from the way the bounds are used: they are reported and interpreted to two decimal places, so variation below 0.01 cannot alter any interpretation of the results. The full simulation is then replicated N_REPLICATIONS times with different random seeds and all other parameters unchanged, and for each of the eight metrics the module reports the largest variation in the CI95 upper bound observed between replications. If that variation is below the declared target for every metric, the current N_ITER is sufficient at this corpus size; a metric whose bound is identical across all replications indicates a wide margin of sufficiency. Where the target is not met, increase N_ITER and re-run Modules 3 → 5.

This module requires Modules 0 → 4 to have been executed in the current session: it reuses the metric functions and parameters already in the global environment and does not read the Excel file. Replication 1 uses the same seed as Module 3, so its upper bounds are compared against report_df as an automatic check that the replication engine still reproduces the main pipeline exactly. Because scenarios live in separate Excel files, run this module once per scenario. Runtime scales linearly with N_REPLICATIONS — roughly ten times a single Module 4 run at the default setting.

```{r module-05-stability}
# Checks whether the iteration count is large enough by replicating the full
# simulation with different seeds and measuring how far BOTH ends of the CI95
# move between replications. Also estimates the iteration count that would be
# needed to reach the declared target precision.
#
# REQUIRES Modules 0 -> 4 in the current session. Reuses .simulate_matrix()
# from Module 3 and .metrics_table(), .ci_lo(), .ci_hi(), metric_names from
# Module 4. Does not read the Excel file and does not touch sims_df/report_df.

# ******************************************
# Parameters
# ******************************************
N_ITER_CHECK     <- N_ITER   # iterations per replication. Defaults to the main
                             # experiment. Override with a literal (e.g. 80000L)
                             # to explore what-if scenarios; when it differs from
                             # N_ITER the consistency check against report_df is
                             # skipped, since replication 1 no longer reproduces
                             # the stored run.

N_REPLICATIONS   <- 10L      # independent replications, each of N_ITER_CHECK
                             # iterations with a different seed. This is NOT the
                             # iteration count: N_ITER_CHECK defines the empirical
                             # distribution, N_REPLICATIONS measures how
                             # reproducible its bounds are. Cost grows as
                             # N_REPLICATIONS x N_ITER_CHECK. Keep it fixed if you
                             # compare Range values across runs: the sufficiency
                             # estimate below assumes it unchanged.

TARGET_PRECISION <- 0.01     # maximum acceptable spread of a bound across
                             # replications, on the metric scale. 0.01 = bounds
                             # are read to two decimals, so anything below this
                             # cannot change the interpretation.
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Dependency check
# ******************************************
.needed <- c("corpus_df", "levels_k", "probs_k", "N_ITER", "SEED",
             "metric_names", ".simulate_matrix", ".metrics_table",
             ".ci_lo", ".ci_hi")
.absent <- .needed[!vapply(.needed, exists, logical(1))]
if (length(.absent))
  stop("Module 5 requires Modules 0-4 to be run first. Missing: ",
       paste(.absent, collapse = ", "))
rm(.needed, .absent)
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Replication engine
# ******************************************
# No simulation or metric logic is restated here: generation comes from
# .simulate_matrix() (Module 3), the metrics table from .metrics_table() and the
# bounds from .ci_lo()/.ci_hi() (Module 4).

bound_keys <- paste(rep(metric_names, each = 2L),
                    c("CI95_Lo", "CI95_Hi"), sep = "|")

.row_min <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
.row_max <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else max(x, na.rm = TRUE)

.bounds_one_run <- function(seed, n_iter) {
  sim <- .simulate_matrix(n_iter = n_iter, seed = seed)

  # Metrics are computed in blocks of columns so that peak memory stays bounded
  # when n_iter is large. Blocking cannot affect the result: the whole matrix is
  # generated in a single call before any metric is computed.
  blocks <- split(seq_len(n_iter), ceiling(seq_len(n_iter) / 2000L))

  m <- purrr::map(blocks, function(idx)
        .metrics_table(as.data.frame(sim[, idx, drop = FALSE]),
                       corpus_df$label_bin)) |>
       (\(z) do.call(rbind, z))()

  # 2 x 8 matrix flattened column-major, i.e. Lo/Hi paired within each metric.
  out <- vapply(metric_names,
                function(nm) c(.ci_lo(m[[nm]]), .ci_hi(m[[nm]])),
                numeric(2))
  setNames(as.vector(out), bound_keys)
}
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Run replications
# ******************************************
# Replication 1 reuses SEED so it reproduces the run reported by Module 4.
# The remaining seeds are drawn from a stream initialised with SEED itself:
# widely dispersed rather than consecutive, and fully recoverable from SEED
# alone, so the whole stability check stays reproducible.
set.seed(SEED)
seed_vector <- c(SEED, sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, N_REPLICATIONS - 1L))

message("Replicating the full simulation ", N_REPLICATIONS, " times (",
        N_ITER_CHECK, " iterations x ", nrow(corpus_df), " items each)...")

bounds_mat <- purrr::map(seq_along(seed_vector), function(r) {
  t0  <- Sys.time()
  out <- .bounds_one_run(seed_vector[r], N_ITER_CHECK)
  message("  replication ", r, "/", N_REPLICATIONS,
          "  seed = ", seed_vector[r], "  (",
          round(as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")), 1), "s)")
  out
}) |>
  (\(x) do.call(cbind, x))()

colnames(bounds_mat) <- sprintf("rep_%02d", seq_len(N_REPLICATIONS))
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Consistency check against report_df
# ******************************************
.comparable <- exists("sims_df") && exists("report_df") &&
               N_ITER_CHECK == N_ITER &&
               sum(grepl("^iter_", names(sims_df))) == N_ITER

if (.comparable) {
  ref <- c(rbind(setNames(report_df$CI95_Lo, report_df$Metric)[metric_names],
                 setNames(report_df$CI95_Hi, report_df$Metric)[metric_names]))
  delta <- max(abs(bounds_mat[, 1] - ref), na.rm = TRUE)
  if (delta < 1e-12) {
    message("Consistency check passed: replication 1 reproduces both bounds ",
            "of report_df exactly.")
  } else {
    warning("Replication 1 does not reproduce report_df (max abs diff = ",
            signif(delta, 3), "). Reconcile before reporting these results.")
  }
  rm(ref, delta)
} else if (N_ITER_CHECK != N_ITER) {
  message("Consistency check skipped: N_ITER_CHECK (", N_ITER_CHECK,
          ") differs from N_ITER (", N_ITER, ") - what-if mode.")
} else {
  message("Consistency check skipped: sims_df was not produced by Module 3.")
}
rm(.comparable)
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Stability table
# ******************************************
# Required N follows from the 1/sqrt(N) scaling of percentile sampling error:
#   N_required = N_current * (Range_observed / Range_target)^2
# It is an approximation: Range is estimated from N_REPLICATIONS values only,
# and it assumes N_REPLICATIONS is held constant.
stability_df <- dplyr::bind_cols(
  tibble::tibble(
    Metric = rep(metric_names, each = 2L),
    Bound  = rep(c("CI95_Lo", "CI95_Hi"), times = length(metric_names))
  ),
  tibble::as_tibble(bounds_mat),
  tibble::tibble(
    Bound_Min = apply(bounds_mat, 1, .row_min),
    Bound_Max = apply(bounds_mat, 1, .row_max)
  )
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Range        = Bound_Max - Bound_Min,
    Target       = TARGET_PRECISION,
    Meets_Target = Range < TARGET_PRECISION,
    N_Required   = ifelse(
      Meets_Target | is.na(Range) | Range == 0, NA_real_,
      ceiling(N_ITER_CHECK * (Range / TARGET_PRECISION)^2)
    )
  )

message("--- CI95 bound stability across ", N_REPLICATIONS,
        " replications (", N_ITER_CHECK, " iterations each) ---")
print(as.data.frame(
  dplyr::mutate(stability_df,
                dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))
), row.names = FALSE)
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Verdict and recommendation
# ******************************************
.round_up <- function(x) {
  k <- 10^(floor(log10(x)) - 1L)
  ceiling(x / k) * k
}

.w <- which.max(stability_df$Range)
message("")
message("  Target precision       : ", TARGET_PRECISION)
message("  Largest range observed : ", signif(stability_df$Range[.w], 3),
        "  (", stability_df$Metric[.w], " ", stability_df$Bound[.w], ")")
.exact <- stability_df$Range == 0 & !is.na(stability_df$Range)
if (any(.exact))
  message("  Identical in all replications: ",
          paste(stability_df$Metric[.exact], stability_df$Bound[.exact],
                collapse = ", "))

if (all(stability_df$Meets_Target, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  message("  ", N_ITER_CHECK,
          " iterations are sufficient at the declared target precision.")
  N_SUGGESTED <- N_ITER_CHECK
} else {
  .fail <- stability_df[!stability_df$Meets_Target, ]
  N_SUGGESTED <- .round_up(1.2 * max(.fail$N_Required, na.rm = TRUE))
  message("  Target not met for: ",
          paste(.fail$Metric, .fail$Bound, sep = " ", collapse = ", "))
  message("  Estimated requirement: ",
          format(max(.fail$N_Required, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",",
                 scientific = FALSE),
          " iterations (driven by ", .fail$Metric[which.max(.fail$N_Required)],
          " ", .fail$Bound[which.max(.fail$N_Required)], ")")
  message("  Suggested value, 20% margin: N_ITER_CHECK <- ",
          format(N_SUGGESTED, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), "L")
  message("  Re-run this chunk with that value to confirm before changing N_ITER.")
  rm(.fail)
}
rm(.exact)
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Provenance block
# ******************************************
# Everything needed to reproduce this check from SEED alone.
stability_meta <- tibble::tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Corpus items", "Positive items", "Prevalence",
    "Simulation distribution (probs_k)",
    "Iterations per replication (N_ITER_CHECK)",
    "Iterations in main experiment (N_ITER)",
    "Replications (N_REPLICATIONS)", "Target precision",
    "Base seed (SEED)", "Seed derivation", "Replication seeds",
    "Largest range observed", "Bound with largest range",
    "All bounds meet target", "Suggested iterations",
    "R version", "Run timestamp"
  ),
  Value = c(
    format(nrow(corpus_df)),
    format(sum(corpus_df$label_bin == "positive", na.rm = TRUE)),
    format(round(mean(corpus_df$label_bin == "positive", na.rm = TRUE), 4)),
    paste(levels_k, round(probs_k, 4), sep = "=", collapse = " | "),
    format(N_ITER_CHECK), format(N_ITER),
    format(N_REPLICATIONS), format(TARGET_PRECISION), format(SEED),
    "set.seed(SEED); c(SEED, sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, N_REPLICATIONS - 1))",
    paste(seed_vector, collapse = ", "),
    format(signif(stability_df$Range[.w], 3)),
    paste(stability_df$Metric[.w], stability_df$Bound[.w]),
    if (all(stability_df$Meets_Target, na.rm = TRUE)) "yes" else "no",
    format(N_SUGGESTED, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
    R.version.string,
    format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  )
)

message("--- Provenance ---")
print(as.data.frame(stability_meta), row.names = FALSE)
rm(.w)
# ******************************************
```

```{r module-05-save}
# Writes the provenance block and stability_df to the Stability sheet.
# Run only if you want them saved. Requires module-05-stability first.

# ******************************************
# Write Stability to Excel
# ******************************************
SH_STAB <- "Stability"
wb      <- openxlsx::loadWorkbook(EXCEL_PATH)

if (SH_STAB %in% names(wb)) openxlsx::removeWorksheet(wb, SH_STAB)
openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, SH_STAB)

hs        <- openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold",
                                   fgFill = "#D9EAD3", border = "Bottom")
num_style <- openxlsx::createStyle(numFmt = "0.0000")
int_style <- openxlsx::createStyle(numFmt = "#,##0")

# Provenance first, metric table below it with one blank row in between.
openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_STAB, stability_meta, startRow = 1,
                    headerStyle = hs)

start_stab <- nrow(stability_meta) + 3L
openxlsx::writeData(wb, SH_STAB, stability_df, startRow = start_stab,
                    headerStyle = hs)

body_rows <- (start_stab + 1L):(start_stab + nrow(stability_df))
col_dec    <- which(names(stability_df) %in%
                      c(colnames(bounds_mat), "Bound_Min", "Bound_Max",
                        "Range", "Target"))
col_int    <- which(names(stability_df) == "N_Required")

openxlsx::addStyle(wb, SH_STAB, num_style, rows = body_rows,
                   cols = col_dec, gridExpand = TRUE)

                   cols = col_int, gridExpand = TRUE)

                       cols = seq_len(ncol(stability_df)), widths = "auto")

openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, EXCEL_PATH, overwrite = TRUE)
```

# Output Excel file description

The Excel file acts as both input and output container and is updated in place at the end of each module that writes results. Two exceptions produce a derived file instead of modifying the original: Module 1 saves to \[original\]\_synthetic.xlsx when it generates a corpus, and the heterogeneous-classifiers chunk saves to \[original\]\_hetero.xlsx. In both cases EXCEL_PATH is updated so subsequent modules follow the new file.

By the end of a complete pipeline run the file contains the following sheets:

Spec — Unchanged from the input. Contains the corpus parameters (n_items, Label, Proportion) used to generate the synthetic corpus and to define the simulation distribution.

Corpus — The labelled dataset used as gold standard. Populated either by Module 1 (synthetic generation) or manually by the user. Contains at minimum ID and Label, optionally Title and Abstract.

Simulations — Contains the full Monte Carlo simulation matrix: one row per corpus item, one column per iteration (iter_0001 … iter_N), plus an ID column. Written by Module 3, which overwrites the sheet on every run. If Module 3 is not executed the sheet retains its previous content, which Module 4 reads directly. Two auxiliary chunks also write here, replacing the iteration columns with their own: validation-known-cases writes the four known-outcome vectors, and heterogeneous-classifiers writes one column per simulated reviewer.

Reporting — The empirical baseline summary table, one row per metric. Columns: Metric, Mean, Median, SD, CI95_Lo, CI95_Hi, NA_pct. Written by Module 4 and overwritten on each run.

Inspection (optional) — Written only if the inspection-save chunk is executed. Contains the confusion matrix (TP, TN, FP, FN) and the eight metrics for each column of the current sims_df, labelled by column name. Used to inspect individual iterations or classifiers in detail, and to verify metric calculations against the known-outcome cases.

Stability (optional) — Written only if the module-05-save chunk is executed. Documents that the iteration count used in the main experiment is large enough for this corpus, and does not affect any result reported by Modules 1–4.The sheet holds two blocks.The upper block is a provenance record: corpus size, positive count and prevalence, the label probabilities used to simulate (`probs_k`) — the entry that identifies which scenario produced the file — the iteration count used in the check (`N_ITER_CHECK`) alongside the one used in the main experiment (`N_ITER`), the number of replications, the declared target precision, the base seed, the rule by which the remaining seeds are derived from it, the resulting seed vector, the largest range observed and the bound that produced it, whether every bound met the target, the suggested iteration count, the R version, and a run timestamp.Because the seeds are recoverable from SEED alone, these entries are sufficient to reproduce the whole check. Below it, separated by a blank row, sits the stability table: sixteen rows, one for each combination of the eight metrics and the two ends of the confidence interval, identified by the Metric and Bound columns. For each row the sheet records the bound obtained in every replication (rep_01 … rep_K), its minimum and maximum across replications (Bound_Min, Bound_Max), the resulting Range, the declared Target, a logical Meets_Target, and N_Required — the iteration count that would be needed to bring that bound within target, estimated from the 1/√N scaling of percentile sampling error and left empty where the target is already met. A Range of exactly zero indicates a bound that was identical in every replication, which points to a wide margin of sufficiency rather than to a borderline result.

# \[OPTIONAL\] Per-case metric verification

This module is not part of the main pipeline. It reads metrics_mat and sims_df produced by the most recent Module 4 run and displays the confusion matrix (TP, TN, FP, FN) and eight metrics for each classifier or iteration, labelled by column name. Although it is designed to be run after the validation module to verify known-outcome cases, it works after any Module 4 execution and can be used to inspect individual classifier results in detail. To save the inspection table to the Excel file, run the inspection-save chunk afterwards.

```{r inspection}
# Displays confusion matrix and 8 metrics for each classifier/iteration
# from the most recent Module 4 run. Works after any Module 4 execution.
# Set SAVE_INSPECTION <- TRUE to write the full table to Excel.

# ******************************************
# Parameters
# ******************************************
SAVE_INSPECTION <- FALSE   # TRUE → writes to Inspection sheet in Excel
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Helper functions
# ******************************************
.binarise_vec <- function(x, pos, neg) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    x %in% pos ~ "positive",
    x %in% neg ~ "negative",
    TRUE        ~ NA_character_
  )
}

.confusion_counts <- function(pred, truth) {
  list(
    TP = sum(pred == "positive" & truth == "positive", na.rm = TRUE),
    TN = sum(pred == "negative" & truth == "negative", na.rm = TRUE),
    FP = sum(pred == "positive" & truth == "negative", na.rm = TRUE),
    FN = sum(pred == "negative" & truth == "positive", na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
# ******************************************

# ******************************************
# Build per-classifier inspection table
# ******************************************
truth     <- corpus_df$label_bin
iter_cols <- setdiff(names(sims_df), "ID")

inspection_df <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(iter_cols), function(i) {
  col  <- iter_cols[i]
  pred <- .binarise_vec(sims_df[[col]], POS_LABELS, NEG_LABELS)
  cm   <- .confusion_counts(pred, truth)

  tibble::tibble(
    Classifier       = col,
    TP               = cm$TP,
    TN               = cm$TN,
    FP               = cm$FP,
    FN               = cm$FN,
    Recall           = metrics_mat[i, "Recall"],
    Specificity      = metrics_mat[i, "Specificity"],
    Precision        = metrics_mat[i, "Precision"],
    NPV              = metrics_mat[i, "NPV"],
    F1               = metrics_mat[i, "F1"],
    F2               = metrics_mat[i, "F2"],
    BalancedAccuracy = metrics_mat[i, "BalancedAccuracy"],
    MCC              = metrics_mat[i, "MCC"]
  )
})

message("─── Per-classifier inspection (", nrow(inspection_df),
        " rows) ───────────────")
print_df <- inspection_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))
print(as.data.frame(print_df), row.names = FALSE)
message("──────────────────────────────────────────────────")
# ******************************************

```
